p: All 9 Mongoose models follow consistent development patterns to ensure maintainability and predictability across the codebase. Each schema definition includes automatic timestamps for createdAt and updatedAt tracking, field validation through required, enum, min, and max constraints, database indexes on frequently queried fields for performance optimization, and a toJSON transform that removes internal fields like __v and sensitive fields like passwords from serialized output.

Models are named using PascalCase convention with corresponding source files in camelCase. Each model uses appropriate Mongoose data types including String, Number, Boolean, Array, ObjectId references, and embedded subdocuments where appropriate. Sensible default values are provided for optional fields to ensure data consistency when documents are created without specifying all fields.

The schema design emphasizes data integrity through validation rules at the database level. Required fields prevent incomplete records, enum constraints restrict field values to predefined options, and numeric constraints like min and max ensure values fall within acceptable ranges. These validations provide a safety net beyond client-side and controller-level validation.

The Crop model stores agricultural crop data with comprehensive field definitions. The name field is required and unique, serving as the primary identifier for each crop entry. The category field uses an enumeration restricted to eight agricultural classifications: vegetable, fruit, grain, legume, herb, nut, oilseed, and ornamental.

Descriptive fields include a detailed description providing comprehensive cultivation information, growingSeason specifying optimal planting and harvesting periods, soilType indicating preferred ground conditions, waterNeeds describing irrigation requirements, and daysToMaturity as a numeric value representing the typical cultivation duration.

The image field stores a URL string pointing to the crop photograph for visual reference. Additional info fields accommodate extended metadata for future extensibility. The model supports full CRUD operations through the API endpoints, with category-based filtering enabling organized browsing of the crop database.

The Product model stores marketplace items with fields designed for e-commerce functionality. The name and description provide basic product identification with search support. The category field uses an enumeration including seed, fertilizer, pesticide, equipment, organic, and other values for marketplace classification and filtering.

The price field uses Number type with a minimum value of 0 to prevent negative pricing. The stock field tracks inventory quantity with a default value of 0, preventing out-of-stock items from being displayed incorrectly. The images array supports multiple product photographs stored as URL strings for gallery display.

The isFeatured boolean flag enables promotional display on the homepage, allowing administrators to highlight selected products. Rating information aggregates user feedback for quality indication. Category filtering enables organized catalog browsing, and featured product queries support marketing use cases.

The User model stores authentication records with comprehensive user management fields. The name field stores the user display name. The email field has a unique index with automatic lowercase conversion for case-insensitive matching. The password field is hashed via bcryptjs pre-save hook and is excluded from JSON output through the toJSON transform method.

The role field uses an enumeration with user and admin values, defaulting to user for new registrations. The phone and address fields enable profile completeness for personalized features. The avatar field stores a profile image URL. Timestamps track account creation and last update.

The comparePassword instance method uses bcrypt.compare for secure login verification, providing constant-time comparison resistant to timing attacks. This method is called during the login process to validate credentials without exposing the hashed password value.

The Blog model manages published content with title, content, author identification, tags for categorization, and image for featured visuals. Timestamps track publication and update dates. The model supports search functionality through text queries on the title and content fields.

The Inquiry model handles contact form submissions with name, email, phone, message content, and isRead flag for tracking submission status. Administrators can view unread submissions and mark them as read after processing, enabling organized communication workflow management.

The Testimonial model displays user feedback with name, role, content, image, and rating fields including star rating for quality feedback. The FAQ model manages frequently asked questions with question, answer, and ordered display positioning for structured presentation.

The Service model lists platform offerings with title, description, icon, features array, and isActive flag for controlling visibility. The Gallery model manages media assets with title, image URL, and category filter. The Analytics model tracks page views with path identification and count aggregation for usage analysis.

Routes are defined in separate files organized by resource type following consistent naming conventions. Each route file creates an Express Router instance, defines HTTP method handlers with their corresponding middleware and controller functions, and exports the router for mounting in server.js under the /api/resource-name URL pattern.

The architecture clearly separates concerns across three layers. Route files define the HTTP interface including URL structure and HTTP methods. Middleware handles cross-cutting concerns like authentication and authorization. Controller files contain the business logic implementation for each endpoint.

The asyncHandler utility wrapper eliminates repetitive try-catch blocks in controller functions. It returns a Promise that automatically catches any errors and forwards them to the Express global error handler via next(), ensuring consistent error propagation without duplicated error handling code.

The CropController handles all crop-related operations with standard CRUD endpoints. GET /api/crops lists all crops with optional query parameter filtering. GET /api/crops/:id retrieves a single crop by its MongoDB identifier. POST /api/crops creates a new crop entry with admin authentication. PUT /api/crops/:id updates an existing crop. DELETE /api/crops/:id removes a crop from the database.

The ProductController mirrors this pattern with additional category filtering support via the query parameter. Products can be filtered by category using GET /api/products?category=seed syntax, enabling organized marketplace browsing.

Both controllers use the asyncHandler wrapper to eliminate try-catch boilerplate and ensure consistent error propagation. Responses follow the standard format with success indicator, data payload, and optional pagination metadata for list endpoints.

The AuthController manages user registration and login operations. POST /api/users/register accepts name, email, and password in the request body, validates required fields, checks for duplicate email addresses returning 409 if found, hashes the password with bcryptjs, creates the User document, generates a JWT token, and returns the token with user data.

POST /api/users/login accepts email and password credentials, performs case-insensitive email lookup, returns 401 if the user is not found or the password does not match, generates a JWT on successful authentication, and returns the token with user data. The error message intentionally does not specify whether the email or password was incorrect to prevent information leakage.

GET /api/users/me returns the current authenticated user profile for token validation and profile display. PUT /api/users/me allows profile updates for the authenticated user. Admin endpoints GET /api/users and DELETE /api/users/:id provide user management capabilities.

Content management controllers handle blog posts, testimonials, FAQs, and services with consistent patterns. Public GET endpoints provide read access with filtering, sorting, and search capabilities. Admin POST, PUT, and DELETE endpoints provide full CRUD capabilities with authentication and authorization verification.

The InquiryController manages contact form submissions with public POST for submission creation and admin GET and DELETE for management with read/unread tracking. The GalleryController handles media items with category filtering for organized display.

The AnalyticsController provides POST endpoint for page view tracking and GET endpoint for aggregated statistics with 30-day retention. The UploadController handles file uploads using multer middleware with file type validation accepting jpg, png, gif, and webp formats and 5MB size limit enforcement.

The auth middleware extracts the JWT token from the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme. It verifies the token using jsonwebtoken.verify with the JWT_SECRET from configuration. On successful verification, it extracts the user ID from the token payload and queries the database to find the corresponding user.

The middleware attaches the found user object to req.user for downstream middleware and controller access. On verification failure, it returns a 401 status with Not authorized message. The middleware handles TokenExpiredError for expired tokens, JsonWebTokenError for malformed tokens, and missing authorization headers appropriately.

This middleware is applied to all protected route definitions, ensuring consistent authentication enforcement across the entire API surface. It serves as the foundation for the platform's role-based access control system, with future extensions planned for granulated permission checking.

The error middleware serves as the centralized error handler for the entire application, catching all errors passed via next(error) from any middleware or controller in the processing pipeline. It uses a custom ErrorResponse class that extends the built-in Error with a statusCode property for HTTP response codes.

Controllers can throw errors with specific HTTP status codes that the handler respects when formatting the response. The handler provides a default status code of 500 for errors without explicit status codes, ensuring all errors produce valid HTTP responses.

The handler returns JSON responses with success:false indicator, the error message in the response body, and in development mode, the stack trace for debugging purposes. Production mode omits stack traces to avoid exposing implementation details to potential attackers.

The asyncHandler utility wraps asynchronous route handler functions to eliminate repetitive try-catch blocks that would otherwise be required in every controller. It accepts a controller function as input and returns a new function that executes the controller and catches any errors, forwarding them to the Express error handling middleware via next().

This utility is used by every controller function across the entire API surface, significantly reducing boilerplate code and ensuring consistent error propagation. It simplifies controller implementation and enhances code readability and maintainability.

The upload utility uses multer for file handling with disk storage configuration that saves uploaded files to the uploads directory. It validates file types against an allowed list of image formats including jpg, png, gif, and webp, and enforces a 5MB file size limit, rejecting files that do not meet these requirements with descriptive error messages.

The configuration utilities in config/db.js and config/config.js centralize database connection management and environment variable access respectively. This approach eliminates scattered process.env references throughout the codebase, improving testability through configuration injection and ensuring consistent configuration access patterns.

The frontend uses Vite 5 with the React plugin for development and production builds. The vite.config.js file configures the development server to proxy /api requests to the backend at localhost:5000, enabling seamless development without CORS configuration. Path resolution is configured with the @ alias pointing to the src directory for clean import statements.

Tailwind CSS runs in JIT mode for optimized stylesheet generation that only includes the utility classes actually used in the source code. PostCSS with autoprefixer handles vendor prefixing for cross-browser CSS compatibility. The entry point src/main.jsx renders the App component wrapped in BrowserRouter.

The build toolchain produces optimized production bundles with code splitting for route-based chunk loading, tree shaking for dead code elimination, asset hashing for cache busting, and CSS extraction for separate stylesheet files. These optimizations ensure fast page loads and efficient caching.

The src directory follows a feature-based organization structure. The context directory contains React context providers for global state management including ThemeContext, AuthContext, and AppContext. The components directory is organized into common subdirectory for 10 reusable UI components, home subdirectory for 10 page section components, and admin subdirectory for 7 admin panel components.

The pages directory contains 13 lazy-loaded page components, each corresponding to a specific route. The hooks directory provides 5 custom React hooks including useAuth, useTheme, useFetch, useForm, and useClickOutside. The animations directory contains Framer Motion variant definitions organized by animation type.

The styles directory holds global CSS with custom properties and theming utilities. The utils directory contains helper functions for common operations. The constants directory stores static data including navigation link definitions, feature flags, and configuration constants used across the application.

The application defines 15 routes using React Router DOM. Public routes include the home page at the root path, about, crops, products, blog list, blog detail with ID parameter, gallery, contact, and FAQ pages. Authentication routes include login, register, and profile pages.

Admin routes are nested under the /admin/ prefix with sub-routes for the dashboard overview, crops management, products management, blogs management with rich text editing, inquiries management with status tracking, users management, and platform settings.

All page components are lazy-loaded using React.lazy with a Suspense wrapper that displays a loading spinner during chunk loading. This code splitting approach reduces the initial bundle size and improves page load performance. A wildcard route at the end matches any undefined paths and displays a custom NotFound page.

The ThemeProvider manages the application's dark and light theme switching using React context. It stores the user's theme preference in localStorage for persistence across browser sessions. The provider applies the dark class to the HTML element for Tailwind CSS dark mode integration, and exposes a toggleTheme function for manual theme switching.

The initial theme value is read from localStorage on application mount. If no saved preference exists, the provider defaults to the system preference detected via the prefers-color-scheme media query, ensuring the theme matches the user's operating system settings by default.

All components access the theme state through the useTheme custom hook, which returns the current theme value, the toggle function, and a boolean isDark flag for conditional rendering. This consistent API enables theme-aware styling throughout the entire component tree.

The AuthProvider manages the complete authentication lifecycle from application initialization through logout. On mount, it checks localStorage for an existing JWT token and validates it by calling the GET /api/users/me endpoint. It provides user state object, loading indicator, login function, register function, and logout function to all child components through React context.

The login function stores the received JWT token in localStorage and configures the Axios default Authorization header for automatic token attachment on subsequent API requests. The logout function removes the token from localStorage, clears the Axios header, and resets all authentication state to initial values.

The provider monitors for 401 responses through the Axios response interceptor, automatically clearing invalid tokens and redirecting to the login page when sessions expire. Protected routes use the authentication state to conditionally render content or redirect unauthenticated users.

The AppProvider manages cross-cutting application state including page loading indicators and alert notification system. The alert system supports auto-dismiss timers for success and error messages, providing consistent user feedback across the application without requiring each component to manage its own notification state.

Providers are nested in a specific hierarchical order to ensure correct context availability. ThemeProvider wraps AuthProvider wraps AppProvider, with ThemeProvider as the outermost layer ensuring theme context is available to all providers and components. AuthProvider provides authentication state that AppProvider and page components depend on.

The combined provider setup is exported as an AppProviders wrapper component for cleaner composition in App.jsx. This nesting order reduces prop drilling, ensures consistent provider ordering, and provides a scalable state management architecture for the application.
